text:
Release

Department of Energy, Office of the Premier

May 25, 2026

FREDERICTON (GNB) – The government has released a comprehensive action plan in response to recommendations identified in the recent review of NB Power, outlining a long-term strategy to provide more stable and affordable rates, strengthen accountability and fiscal sustainability, and better position New Brunswick for future growth in the energy sector.

The comprehensive review, which was launched in April 2025, focused on four areas: financial sustainability, governance and utility structure, customer expectations, and investor attractiveness and strategic partnerships. Three independent leads were identified to conduct a transparent, collaborative and evidence-based review while engaging with New Brunswickers and stakeholders.

The review followed years of rising electricity costs and growing concern from New Brunswickers about affordability and spikes in bills. The government implemented a 10 per cent rebate on power bills to help mitigate the rate increases.

The action plan focuses on modernizing the utility so it can operate more efficiently, manage future growth responsibly, and help provide more stable and competitive rates over the long term.

"New Brunswickers are worried about affordability and frustrated by rising power bills,” said Premier Susan Holt. “This review made it clear that maintaining the status quo is not an option. We are taking a comprehensive approach to transforming NB Power so it can deliver reliable service, better manage costs and remain financially sustainable as demand for electricity continues to grow. At the same time, New Brunswick has an opportunity to play a larger role in Canada’s evolving electricity system and help power growth across the Maritimes. The actions we are taking today are about protecting ratepayers while positioning our province to compete and succeed in the clean energy economy.”

The government is acting on all 50 of the recommendations in the review. Recommendations are grouped under eight major outcomes focused on improving governance, modernizing regulation, strengthening long-term energy planning, improving organizational performance and ensuring disciplined management of major infrastructure projects.

Key actions include:

Developing a new long-term provincial energy policy aligned with NB Power’s future needs and the province’s economic growth objectives.

Reviewing and modernizing the Electricity Act and broader energy regulatory framework to improve transparency, accountability and long-term planning.

Creating an energy sector consumer advocate’s office to better represent residential and small business customers.

Advancing discussions around greater regional co-operation and integration among utilities in the Maritimes, including exploring the concept of a Maritime independent system operator.

Improving accountability with respect to performance measurement, staffing reviews, project management and customer service within NB Power.

Strengthening oversight and financial planning for major projects such as those at the Mactaquac and Belledune generating stations.

Improving the performance of the Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station through planning, accountability, clear metrics and relationship-building.

Energy Minister René Legacy said the plan recognizes the urgency of affordability concerns and the importance of preparing the province for increasing electricity demand and the clean-energy transition.

“New Brunswick is already a critical part of the regional electricity system, and we have an opportunity to build on that strength,” said Legacy. “But to do that, we need a utility that is modern, financially sustainable and capable of making smart long-term decisions. This action plan creates a clear path forward to improve reliability, support competitive rates and ensure NB Power is positioned to meet the needs of New Brunswickers for decades to come.”

Implementation of the plan is already underway in several areas. Progress will be tracked through quarterly updates, with results being made available to the public online.

text:
The Canadian Coast Guard is exploring a new generation of clean energy technologies to displace its existing diesel generators with support from three University of Victoria (UVic)-based research institutes as part of a new project announced last month.

The project is the first of a series of “innovation challenges” coming out of the BC Marine Energy and Decarbonzation Hub, a collaboration between Accelerating Community Energy Transformation (ACET), Pacific Regional Institute for Marine Energy Discovery (PRIMED) and the Institute for Integrated Energy Systems (IESVic) with the Center for Ocean Applied Sustainable Technologies (COAST).

In April, the group announced details of four companies that will receive funding through the Innovate BC Integrated Marketplace program, along with lab space and technical support from ACET researchers, to develop and test tailored solutions that advance the Coast Guard’s goal to electrify its operations in remote coastal areas of B.C.

“Through this [innovation] challenge, we’re tapping into BC’s innovation and technology sector and cutting-edge solutions developed right here at home,” states Ravi Kahlon, Minister of Jobs and Economic Growth.

Although it’s still early days, this signals a sea change in the province’s marine renewable energy sector, which has long relied on expertise, equipment and project experience imported from the US, UK and Europe.

“As demand for renewable energy grows and people look for homegrown solutions from local experts they can trust, UVic has three decades of marine energy expertise to draw from,” says Lisa Kalynchuk, the University’s vice president of research and innovation. “Through the BC Marine Energy and Decarbonization Hub, we’re proud to contribute solutions that reduce diesel dependence, strengthen our ocean economy and empower coastal industries, operators and communities across the province.”

Decades in the making

Since the early 2000s, UVic researchers have worked closely with provincial and regional partners to advance marine renewable energy in B.C.

A leading figure behind this push is Brad Buckham, professor and chair of UVic’s department of mechanical engineering, whose early work focused on understanding wave-energy potential off Vancouver Island through the West Coast Wave Initiative (WCWI).

The initiative brought together researchers, industry and government partners to gather some of the first long-term wave and tidal resource data on Canada’s west coast.

“We thought of the broad gaps of knowledge foundations that people need—like resource assessments, wave energy modeling, coastal engineering work and deploying wave monitoring buoys,” Buckham recalls. “While working with agencies like Natural Resources Canada, Western Economic Development and BC Ministry of Energy and Climate Solutions, we began building trust by showing we can do good work and mobilize knowledge in a way that people can use it.”

More than a decade and many projects later, Buckham found himself in good company at IESVic with another colleague from mechanical engineering, professor Curran Crawford, who specialized in tidal and wind energy systems and had been working as a consultant on rotor design and optimization.

The two began collaborating on offshore wind energy projects—and PRIMED was born shortly after, with Buckham and Crawford co-directing.

“PRIMED is a team of researchers, engineers and facilitators that sits between the communities trying to adopt marine energy technology, the regulators overseeing the space that technology works in, and the technology providers that are trying to make those devices work better.” Buckham explains. “This is a unique approach within Canada for ocean renewable energy. Our work gives communities a real opportunity to meaningfully engage in the transformation of their energy systems.”

The team’s first project was with the Hesquiaht First Nation, analyzing how a small hydroelectric plant could work within the community’s existing energy system and whether the addition of tidal power could help end their reliance on diesel fuel.

Their research lab has since grown into a team of 13 full-time employees with 15 marine resource monitoring buoys currently collecting data along the west coast and a slate of projects—from the Quatsino Narrows to Haida Gwaii—on the go.

Now an independent division of ACET specializing in marine renewable energy, PRIMED’s recent milestones include playing a formative role in the creation of Canada’s Marine Energy Atlas, and receiving a $1 million grant from TD Bank Group to support the Mowachaht/Muchalaht First Nation’s effort to re-occupy the ancestral village site from which it was displaced by harnessing the power of waves.

“In the early years for Brad and me, our focus was more of a pure engineering optimization approach that was curiosity-driven. We still get excited talking about the fundamental physics modeling and design stuff,” Crawford shares. “But for both of us, working with coastal communities was a gateway to a whole realm of learning about what this technology can do for people by integrating it into existing energy systems.”

This whole-system approach is something the two co-founders acknowledge came from their long-standing membership in IESVic, which first housed WCWI and then PRIMED. The interdisciplinary research centre was also foundational for ACET, created in 2023.

“You have to understand the ocean, mechanical systems, electrical controls, grid integration,” says Bryson Robertson, IESVic’s new director. “But you also have to understand communities, policy and perception. That’s systems thinking.”

Primed for growth

The role of marine renewable energy in helping Canada reach its net-zero goals is primed for significant growth, according to Crawford.

“Different technologies will play a different role at different scales and in different places, but there are many unharnessed terawatts of power along Canadian coastlines,” he says. “Assuming it’s done correctly in collaboration with communities, I would expect to see Canada deploying larger-scale wave, tidal and offshore wind platforms over the next five to 10 years.”

To get there, much work needs to be done to bring these nascent technologies to market, integrate them into existing power grids and demonstrate their value for and harmony with communities if implemented properly, which are key priorities for the BC Marine Energy and Decarbonization Hub.

“The projects the hub supports aren’t just about eliminating diesel use—they’re about materializing benefits for people: economic development, community resilience, environmental sustainability,” says Buckham.

“In this regard, the hub isn’t as focused on changing habits as it is on creating new opportunities. It’s a strong example of how university research and innovation translates into jobs and companies that make a difference for communities.”

Research undertaken through the BC Marine Energy and Decarbonization Hub is funded in part by the Canada First Research Excellence Fund, as part of the University of Victoria-led Accelerating Community Energy Transformation (ACET) Initiative.

text:
Within the framework of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), two interwoven challenges have long plagued low-income regions: eradicating extreme poverty (SDG 1) and ensuring universal access to clean, modern energy (SDG 7). According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the number of people without access to electricity rose by nearly 20 million in 2022, reaching approximately 775 million, marking the first global increase since the IEA began tracking this metric two decades ago. This reversal was disproportionately concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, a region hard-hit by the pandemic, global inflation, and ongoing energy crises1. While the figure declined to 750 million in 2023, sub-Saharan Africa remains mired in a severe energy access gap, accounting for 80% of the world’s population without electricity2.

Globally, over 2 billion people still depend on coal, solid biomass, or kerosene to meet daily cooking and heating needs, with no access to clean energy infrastructure. Over half of this population resides in Africa, and alarmingly, toxic smoke from these polluting fuels ranks as the second leading cause of premature death across the continent—with women and children bearing the brunt of these fatalities, primarily in sub-Saharan Africa3. For women, the hours spent daily gathering basic fuels directly constrain their access to education, employment opportunities, and economic independence. This dual poverty nexus, where income poverty restricts access to efficient energy, and energy poverty in turn suppresses productivity (e.g., disabling industrial operations, disrupting schools and clinics) and perpetuates intergenerational deprivation4, has become a bottleneck for equitable development.

For China, the per capita residential electricity consumption reached nearly 1000 kWh in 2024, and the number of natural gas users hit 560 million. China’s ranking for “Getting Electricity” in the World Bank’s Doing Business report rose to 12th place in the world5. However, back in 2015, China had only finished constructing power infrastructure in all areas without electricity access6. Over the following years, although grid connectivity has improved greatly, energy poverty persists in a different form. The challenge has evolved from a crisis of access to one of affordability. Previous research categorizes energy poverty into consumption energy poverty and livelihood energy poverty based on household energy expenditure statistics. It finds China’s overall energy poverty rate is 18.9%. Of this total, 54% is livelihood energy poverty characterized by electricity consumption below basic needs. This is driven by grid access, electronic device ownership, and income levels. The remaining 46% is consumption energy poverty, defined by excessive electricity spending relative to income, driven by income levels and electricity prices. Central China has the highest overall energy poverty rate at 22.63%, while western China faces a more severe livelihood energy poverty problem, accounting for 11.11% of its 19.22% total energy poverty rate7. Due to relatively low per capita income, energy poverty is particularly severe in rural areas. Many rural households depended on coal for heating and crop straw burning for waste disposal8, creating a vicious cycle: inefficient energy use fueled air pollution, which raised health burdens and reduced labor capacity9. Persistent poverty, in turn, left communities unable to invest in clean energy alternatives10. Traditional poverty alleviation strategies, such as industrial transfer or direct subsidies, often failed to break this cycle: industrial projects risked exacerbating environmental degradation11, while direct subsidies rarely addressed the root of energy inefficiency. By 2014, when China launched its Photovoltaic Poverty Alleviation Program (PPAP) as part of the Ten Key Precision Poverty Alleviation Programs12, the need for a solution that synergized poverty reduction and ecological protection had become urgent.

PPAP emerged as a pioneering policy innovation: it leveraged the abundant solar resources in rural impoverished areas to build distributed photovoltaic (PV) power stations, installed on residential rooftops or idle collective land, integrating clean energy generation with targeted income support. Unlike conventional PV projects (which prioritize energy supply alone) or traditional poverty alleviation (which focuses on short-term income transfers), PPAP’s core logic was dual-purpose: under its “self-consumption with surplus grid feed-in” model, households sell excess electricity to the national grid at subsidized tariffs13, directly boosting disposable income14; simultaneously, widespread PV adoption reduced reliance on fossil fuels, driving rural energy upgrading and industrial clean transformation. By 2017, when the National Energy Administration (NEA) expanded PPAP to 236 counties nationwide (establishing 8,689 village-level stations with 4.19 million kilowatts of installed capacity)15,16, the program had become a test case for whether clean energy could serve as a “bridge” between poverty eradication and sustainable development.

Despite PPAP’s policy significance, existing research has failed to fully and precisely capture its value. Quantitative research on PPAP can be categorized into four types based on methodology: (1) Theoretical modeling and analysis17,18, such as adopting game theory models to verify the policy’s sustainability; (2) Indicator-based evaluation19,20,21, including the construction of an evaluation framework to assess PPAP’s social benefits; (3) Numerical methods and simulation22,23,24,25,26, which quantify photovoltaic benefits by multiplying electricity generation by electricity prices and emission indices; (4) Econometric and quasi-experimental approaches14,27,28, which employ quasi-experimental designs and econometric models to evaluate the household benefits of photovoltaic policies. Despite these diverse approaches, each methodological type has inherent limitations: theoretical research lacks empirical data validation; indicator-based evaluation systems are subjective and fail to address the endogeneity issue of indicators; the application of electricity prices and emission factors in numerical method research introduces significant measurement errors and overlooks the complex indirect benefits brought by the policy. While empirical model-based research can resolve these issues, existing empirical studies focus primarily on economic aspects, lack relevant environmental evidence, and ignore the systemic interdependence between economic growth and environmental improvement.

Most existing studies adopt numerical methods, focusing on the market value and carbon reductions associated with photovoltaic power generation. However, the true benefits of PV projects stretch well beyond such direct generation-related gains. Large-scale PV projects yield substantial indirect benefits, including boosting employment, stimulating commercial activity, and fostering residents’ clean energy habits — value that goes beyond megawatt metrics. Against this backdrop, our study addresses a critical gap: it uses high-resolution remote sensing data and county-level economic data in empirical models to quantify PPAP’s dual effects on the economy and the environment. Building on existing economic research, we further explore the underlying mechanisms through which PV deployment contributes to poverty reduction, including income growth, employment creation, and enterprise entry. For the environmental dimension, we leverage satellite data to provide empirical evidence of PPAP’s environmental benefits. At a time when global policymakers are seeking scalable models for green poverty alleviation, understanding PPAP’s real-world impacts is not only academically meaningful, but also provides an evidence-based blueprint for aligning two critical global objectives: poverty alleviation and environmental sustainability. This study posits two central hypotheses: first, the large-scale implementation of the PPAP acts as a driver for local economic growth by increasing GDP; and second, the construction of photovoltaic facilities in impoverished areas effectively mitigates air pollution levels.

In order to quantify the economic and environmental impacts of PPAP policy, we utilize gross domestic product (GDP) and ambient sulfur dioxide (SO₂) concentration as proxy variables for economic performance and environmental pollution. GDP is the most standardized and direct economic indicator, and it is more accessible and comprehensive compared with other economic data. While air pollution consists of multiple components (SO2, NOx, and PM2.5), the sources of SO₂ are more straightforward than those of other air pollutants. In 2013, China’s SO₂ and NOₓ emissions were 20.439 and 22.273 million tons, of which 85% SO₂, 67% NOₓ, and 70% soot came from coal-based fossil fuel combustion29, so SO₂ is more directly affected by the substitution effect of photovoltaic power. We select it to allow the econometric model to capture the fluctuations in air pollutant concentrations caused by the PPAP policy.

We identify PPAP’s dual impacts: economically, it boosts GDP by 2.9% via income growth, job creation, and capital inflows; environmentally, it promotes industrial clean transition and rural energy upgrading, reducing SO₂ concentrations by 4.2 μg/m³. The benefits yielded from these two dimensions vary significantly across regions. We further discuss the policy’s effectiveness and sustainability, offering empirical references and optimization insights for scaling such green poverty reduction models in energy-poor regions globally.

Research scope and overview

Our study focuses on the impoverished counties, treating the implementation of the PPAP as a quasi-natural experiment. Among 832 impoverished counties, 236 listed in “13th Five-Year Plan”15 are designated as the treatment group (PPAP counties), with the remaining counties serving as the control group. Figure 1a and b show the spatial distribution of PPAP coverage and installed capacity, indicating that the policy is concentrated in central and western China. Figure 1c and d detail the initial economic and environmental conditions of all impoverished counties, with orange lines highlighting the PPAP coverage.

To identify the causal effect of PPAP on the economy and environment, we use the difference-in-differences (DID) methodology that compares the changes in policy covered counties before and after PPAP participation with changes in uncovered counties over the same time period. Figure 2 shows a toy model of DID and displays how it measures the treatment effect of a policy. This methodology allows us to subtract out background changes common to both groups and effectively isolates the change in outcomes specifically related to the policy implementation beyond secular trends. Our analysis relies on the parallel trends assumption, which posits that the outcome trajectories in the treatment and control groups would have evolved similarly in the absence of policy intervention. By deriving these estimates from regression models rather than simple subtraction, we are further able to adjust for potential confounding characteristics that may differ between the counties.

Given the potential non-random assignment of treatment status, we must take particular care in using the DID model because human intervention and self-selection factors could confound our results. To mitigate this problem, we further implement a Propensity Score Matching Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) approach to pair treated and untreated counties based on observable county-level characteristics. Specifically, each PPAP-participating county is matched with a non-participating counterpart exhibiting the closest propensity score; these scores are estimated using key economic and environmental covariates, such as government budget, administrative area, financial market development, and precipitation. This matching procedure significantly enhances the comparability of the treatment and control groups by minimizing systematic differences in baseline attributes. Detailed specifications of the econometric models and the sample construction methodology are provided in the Methods section.

Impacts of PPAP on the economy and the environment

By fitting the DID model (Table 1 and Eq. (1)), we find that PPAP did improve GDP and air quality: compared with other impoverished counties, PPAP counties had 2.9% higher GDP growth and 4.249 μg/m³ lower SO₂ concentrations. Re-estimating the baseline regression with the matched sample yielded results that were broadly consistent with our initial findings, indicating that differences in the initial characteristics of the sample do not significantly influence the baseline DID model. To strengthen the credibility of our conclusions, we conducted multiple robustness checks as follows.

Robustness

Substitute dependent variables

To test the robustness of our findings, we re-estimate the main regressions using alternative measures: per capita GDP is used as an alternative indicator of economic development, and ambient NO₂ concentration serves as a substitute measure of air pollution, because it shares similar emission sources with SO230 (see Supplementary Table 1 for results with PM2.5 and CO). Table 2 presents the results of robustness checks using alternative dependent variables. The policy’s positive economic effect strengthens to 5.1%, remaining statistically significant with an effect direction consistent with the baseline. We attribute this larger positive effect on per capita GDP to long-term population outflow in impoverished counties31, which amplifies the estimated impact compared to our initial results. For the alternative measure of ambient NO₂ concentration, the policy’s pollution reduction effect is 1.08 units, still statistically significant and aligned with the baseline direction. Two factors explain the coefficient difference from the baseline: first, SO₂ and NO₂ have differing atmospheric concentrations32; second, PV systems likely reduce pollution by substituting clean energy for coal and gas, a mechanism more impactful for SO₂ than NO₂ because of their different sources32. Importantly, these differences do not undermine the robustness of our baseline findings. Overall, even with adjusted dependent variables, our conclusions hold.

Placeable test

To rule out spurious results from random sampling errors or unobserved confounders, we conduct a placebo test involving 500 random reassignments of treatment and control groups33. The core idea is to simulate a counterfactual scenario of fake policy intervention: if the original policy effect remains statistically significant only under the actual treatment assignment (not in these random simulations), this effectively rules out alternative explanations such as chance matching or confounding interference, thereby enhancing the credibility and scientific rigor of our conclusions. We repeated the random assignment process 500 times, using the same baseline regression each time. Figure 3 presents the resulting coefficients. Our findings indicate that the policy’s promotional effects on economic development and air quality are not accidental or spurious.

Intensity varying DID model

Above, we estimated the overall effect of the PPAP policy. However, not all counties received identical levels of policy subsidies. For instance, in Qinghai province, the installed capacity of PPAP-supported power stations in Chengduo County stands at 11,400 kW, more than twice that of Qilian County (4500 kW), despite the two counties having similar populations and administrative land areas. It is reasonable to infer that if photovoltaic power delivers economic and environmental improvements, counties with higher photovoltaic installation capacity should exhibit stronger policy effects. By measuring the installed capacity of PV power stations and the count of supported households, we can quantify the overall effect of policy intensity on poverty alleviation outcomes. We adopt a generalized DID model (Eq. (3)), where the treatment variable is no longer a binary variable but a continuous variable. Policy intensity is measured by the installed capacity of power stations, the number of households supported, and village-level coverage. Table 3 shows a positive correlation between the intensity of PPAP and both the resulting growth in local per capita GDP and the reduction in local ambient SO₂ concentrations, with the following key findings: for every 10,000 kW of photovoltaic power plant capacity installed through PPAP, per capita GDP increases by 1.5% while SO₂ concentrations decrease by 1.79 μg/m³; each additional 100 registered poverty-stricken villages per county strengthens PPAP’s impact on per capita GDP by 5% and is associated with a 6.77 μg/m³ reduction in SO₂ concentrations; an increase of 10,000 households supported by PPAP raises the policy’s effect on per capita GDP by 9.8% and results in a 10.68 μg/m³ decrease in SO₂ concentrations. All these results are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level.

Economic and ecological trends before and after PPAP

In addition to the baseline results, we conduct the following additional analyses. Based on Figure 2, to construct a counterfactual treatment group (T1counterfactual) for evaluating policy effects, a key assumption is that the treatment and the control group should exhibit parallel trends in outcome variables if the PPAP had not been implemented. This assumption cannot be verified as the treatment group has already been exposed to the policy in reality. However, we can strengthen the validity of our assumption by confirming that the two groups shared similar trends before the policy was introduced. We employ an event-study approach (Eq. (2)), which illustrates how trends between PPAP counties and non-PPAP counties evolve before and after the policy implementation. Figure 4 presents these results. By comparing GDP and SO₂ concentrations between the treatment and control groups, we find no systematic differences throughout the pre-policy period (relative time < 0). In contrast, the trend breaks after PPAP implementation, meaning the lagged terms (relative time ≥ 0) become statistically significant. Specifically, GDP increased by 3% within one year of PPAP implementation, while SO₂ concentrations decreased by more than 4 μg/m³ within two years. Moreover, our findings demonstrate robustness to alternative dependent variables, strengthening the strong relationship between PPAP and improvements in economic and environmental conditions (see Supplementary Fig. 1 for details).

Mechanisms

Income effect

PPAP channels project returns directly into households’ disposable income. Table 4 backs this up: household savings rose 9.5 ± 3.7%, urban per capita disposable income grew 6.7 ± 2.2%, and rural per capita disposable income increased 6.5 ± 2.7%. As these families earn more, their tendency to spend rises, boosting local demand for daily necessities, services, and other goods34. This increased demand drives growth in retail, services, and other industries. Facing higher orders, local firms expand production, upgrade equipment, hire more workers, and increase investments—all of which strengthen capital formation. These steps ultimately fuel local GDP growth.

Employment effect

The construction and operation of photovoltaic power stations create diverse employment opportunities. Following PV policy implementation, both year-end employee counts and urban on-the-job staff numbers rose by 16 ± 11.8%. During the construction phase, significant local labor is required for tasks such as equipment transportation, installation, and debugging, and basic civil engineering, creating short-term, high-intensity labor demand. In the operational phase, long-term stable technical roles and managerial positions provide ongoing employment support35. Labor compensation from increased employment flows to households as wages, raising overall disposable income and ultimately driving GDP growth. Additionally, the policy is shown to promote employment in secondary and tertiary industries, with no significant impact on primary industries such as agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry, and fisheries (see Supplementary Table 3 for details).

Capital inflow effect

PPAP generates stable income and electricity. This dual effect expands the consumer market and improves the power market system. An active consumer market and reliable power supply together create investment location advantages, encouraging outside businesses like commercial firms and service organizations to invest locally36. Table 4 shows that after the policy, annual enterprise registrations increased by 7.3 ± 6.1% (see Supplementary Fig. 2 for additional placebo test). Meanwhile, varied funding models (like government subsidies and bank loans) used in building and running power stations boost local financial markets. Expanding investment demand and improving financial efficiency together drive overall GDP growth. We also find that the annual number of newly registered retail and financial firms increased by 10.0 ± 6.9% and 11.6 ± 8.6%, respectively, further backing up our analysis.

Clean energy transformation in secondary industries

The secondary industry—particularly energy-intensive manufacturing, mining, and heat production and supply—is the primary source of SO₂ emissions, which mainly stem from fossil fuel combustion processes such as coal-fired boilers, industrial kilns, and thermal power generation units30. After being integrated into the power grid, electricity generated by PV stations reduces overall electricity costs through market-based pricing mechanisms. In response, factories substitute their traditional reliance on coal and natural gas with low-sulfur, zero-emission electricity. More PV power in industrial use cuts coal consumption in production, reducing SO₂ emissions. Meanwhile, cost constraints on energy use incentivize pollution-abatement technology upgrades. As a cheap, clean energy source, PV power lowers industrial energy expenses, freeing up funds for environmental protection technologies. Concurrently, local governments often coordinate PV poverty alleviation policies with green industrial transformation initiatives37,38 (e.g., tax incentives for enterprises using clean energy), further motivating firms to proactively reduce fossil fuel dependence.

Due to limitations in accessing enterprise-level data, we validate this mechanism indirectly. We split sample counties into high- and low-secondary-industry groups based on the secondary industry share of GDP in 2016 (As PPAP was implemented in 2017, post-2017 data have already been affected by the policy, which would cause statistical issues if used for grouping to assess policy effects). We then conducted group regressions. If our hypothesis holds, regions with a higher share of secondary industries should see stronger pollution cuts from PPAP. Table 5 supports this: the policy reduces emissions more in the high-secondary-industry regions than low ones, with a statistically significant difference39.

Residential clean energy transition

Household SO₂ emissions mainly come from scattered coal burning and inefficient burning of sulfur-containing fuels40. PPAP helps cut these emissions in two ways: (1) under the self-consumption mode with surplus electricity connected to the grid, PV electricity replaces traditional coal-fired boilers with clean power, directly reducing SO₂ emissions from household coal use; (2) by boosting household income, PPAP helps families afford clean energy tools like electric heaters and induction cookers41. Local electricity price subsidies for PV users also lower the cost of switching to clean energy, motivating households to reduce their use of high-pollution fuels like loose coal and firewood, reducing harmful gas emissions.

Since we lack detailed household data, we validate this mechanism indirectly. We split sample counties into high- and low-income groups based on 2016 rural income averages and conduct group regressions. We hypothesize that residents in lower-income regions are more likely to maintain coal-dependent lifestyles before PPAP42; thus, the lifestyle transitions induced by PPAP should be more pronounced in these areas, leading to greater SO₂ emission reductions. Table 5 confirms this: PPAP reduces SO₂ more in low-income rural areas than in high-income areas, with a statistically significant difference.

Policy Effects by Secondary Industry Share

The secondary industry is both the largest consumer of electricity and the largest source of of polluting gases. Given that PV power stations have increased regional electricity supply, we further verify whether policy benefits vary under different electricity demand conditions. Sample counties are categorized into high- and low-secondary-industry groups based on the share of secondary industry in GDP in 2016. Group regression analysis shows that the policy’s marginal SO₂ emission reduction effect is −5.787 μg/m³ in the high-secondary-industry group, compared to −3.024 μg/m³ in the low-secondary-industry group. In terms of economic effects, the policy treatment effect reaches 4.25% in the low-secondary-industry group, while it is 1.64% (statistically insignificant) in the high-secondary-industry group. These results are presented in Fig. 5.

For regions with a high share of secondary industry, we argue that this high share is a result of the region’s inherent sufficient electricity supply; thus, the implementation of PPAP exerts no significant economic promotion effects on the secondary industry. However, the more abundant green energy facilitates the green transition of the existing heavy industry, leading to a notable emission reduction effect. In contrast, for regions with a low share of secondary industry, the additional electricity supply drives the development of secondary industry, generating significant extra economic benefits. Since the local secondary industry itself is underdeveloped, the emission reduction effect brought by increased electricity supply is significant but less pronounced than that in the high-secondary-industry group.

As a pivotal policy initiative that synergizes two core United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, PPAP holds profound significance for global efforts to break the dual poverty nexus. Our findings offer key insights into several policy-related issues. To understand how PPAP affects people’s well-being, we need to quantify both its direct and indirect effects. Our study shows that PPAP significantly improves air quality, which is critical for assessing the policy’s overall benefits. According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes 6.7 million premature deaths annually, and people in low- and middle-income countries are generally more vulnerable to it43. Existing studies show that long-term exposure to air pollutants such as SO₂ and NO₂ increases the prevalence and severity of asthma44, and using clean energy helps improve household members’ health45.

While PPAP delivers dual economic and environmental benefits across the overall sample, its effectiveness varies significantly across regions. Our findings show that PPAP’s environmental benefits, particularly in terms of marginal contributions, are more significant in counties with high industrial density. As shown in Fig. 5, the policy’s SO₂ emission reduction effect in the high-secondary-industry group is nearly twice as strong as in the low-secondary-industry group. This indicates that PV poverty alleviation acts as a catalyst for green transition in high-industrial areas. Through a stable clean energy supply, it directly reduces enterprises’ pollution emission intensity and improves local environmental quality. Meanwhile, we also find that the policy’s economic benefits are more pronounced in counties with lower secondary industry shares. In other words, while PPAP generates positive impacts on both the economy and the environment, these two types of benefits do not align perfectly. Although we recommend incorporating the policy’s environmental effects into evaluations, policymakers should balance their governance objectives when formulating decisions.

A closer look at the mechanisms behind PPAP’s economic effects reveals a potential vulnerability. Based on our analysis of policy mechanisms, most of these channels rely heavily on direct income increases for residents from power station dividends (see Supplementary Fig. 3 for details). However, the sustainable operation of PPAP faces dual constraints: PV feed-in tariffs are declining due to reduced policy subsidies and intensified market competition, significantly challenging the stability of project returns across the whole lifecycle of these projects. On one hand, rapid reductions in PV costs46,47,48 have intensified market competition, driving down electricity prices and making power station revenues heavily dependent on policy subsidies. On the other hand, while governments use fiscal subsidies to bridge the market price gap to sustain poverty relief effects, such non-market adjustments will increase long-term fiscal burdens49. As early as 2016, reports estimated that the subsidy gap for pilot policies reached 55 billion yuan50, directly impacting fund turnover for station operation and maintenance and dividend expectations for poor households. Data from China’s National Energy Administration51 show that the accumulated subsidy shortfall for photovoltaics reached 45.5 billion yuan by 2017, with this deficit growing year by year. This expanding financial gap has become a challenge, potentially leading to cuts or even the cancellation of subsidies for the PV industry52. To achieve a more sustainable poverty alleviation model, policies should shift from subsidy reliance to self-sustaining models.

In efforts to achieve self-sustaining development via the implementation of PV projects, composite models such as Aquaculture-PV integration and Livestock-PV integration have been validated and promoted in some regions53,54,55. Specifically, Aquaculture-PV Integration involves installing PV panels above aquaculture or agricultural areas, while aquaculture or agricultural activities are sustained beneath the panels. These panels filter intense sunlight and reduce rainfall impact, creating a favorable microenvironment for the organisms or crops below. In turn, the underlying aquaculture or agricultural activities prevent the area from being left idle or overrun by weeds, thereby lowering the operation and maintenance costs of PV power stations. However, our study finds that their market-driven effects on related industries remain limited for PPAP—supporting sectors such as agricultural product processing and cold chain logistics are underdeveloped, with no significant enterprise settlement observed across primary industry sectors. We attribute this limitation to two factors: village-level PV stations built under poverty alleviation programs struggle to attract corporate collaboration, and such composite models pose technical barriers to impoverished areas. To address this, we propose boosting human capital investment through targeted training for villagers on core technologies of these integrated models, and refining government policies to support the industrial chain, such as offering tax incentives, logistics subsidies, and other supportive measures to enterprises engaged in PV-agricultural integration projects. These measures aim to amplify market effects through the clustered development of the “PV + industry” model.

Our study finds PPAP boosts GDP by 2.9%. However, given its large-scale investment, cost-return imbalance risks from the common “prioritizing construction over operation” practice demand attention. Chong et al.‘s research, using the Levelized Cost of Electricity model that includes PV full lifecycle investment costs, found significant provincial differences in PV electricity costs. The highest cost, observed in Hunan Province, reaches 1.23 yuan/kWh56. Factoring in such costs would substantially reduce comprehensive economic returns below initial expectations. Since the National Poverty Alleviation Office has not disclosed the details of fiscal expenditures, we obtained a tender notice for PV projects in Qinghai Province. The notice outlines a plan for the construction of PV power plants with a total capacity of 50.5 megawatts across five counties: Guide, Guinan, Tongde, Xinghai, and Gonghe57. These data is fully consistent with PPAP’s construction targets for these counties, allowing us to confirm that this project falls under the PPAP framework. The notice further specifies that the total investment for this batch of construction is 353.5 million yuan. According to the estimation in our study, the total economic benefits generated by the PPAP in these five counties as of 2020 amounted to 188.4 million yuan. It is evident that even when accounting for the overall economic effect, PPAP’s short-term benefits are considerable but still insufficient to cover the costs. To achieve revenue-cost balance in the future, long-term refined operations will be essential. From an economic standpoint, PPAP is more akin to transfer payments in the short term, while functioning as engines of economic growth in the long term. Consequently, when promoting similar policies, developing countries must give full consideration to their own fiscal conditions and policy objectives.

Data

Policy data

The classification of impoverished counties is based on official government documents62. There are 832 such counties nationwide, with the vast majority located in central and western China. PPAP counties are classified according to the 13th Five-Year Plan15. These documents specify the list of supported counties, including the number of assisted households and the details of PV station construction for each. In this study, there are 236 PPAP counties, all of which are included in the 832 poverty-stricken counties.

Weather data

Rainfall data is collected from a data product providing 5 km resolution global monthly precipitation63,64. Using Google Earth Engine, we calculated global annual average precipitation, disaggregated this by region to each sample county, and generated time-series data covering all samples. In this study, regional precipitation affects concentrations of air pollutants. It also has a strong correlation with regional sunlight conditions, which influences the likelihood of county participation in PPAP.

Air quality data

Pollutant gas concentration data are derived from a data product. This database provides annual ground-level NO₂ and SO₂ concentration data for China at 1–10 km resolution65,66,67. Using ArcGIS, we performed zonal statistics at the county level to generate time-series data. County air quality was measured by the average pollutant gas concentration across each county’s mapped area.

Socio-economic status

We construct a county-level panel dataset of economic indicators, including GDP, industrial structure, per capita land area, government fiscal conditions, and financial investment sourced from the Chinese County Statistical Yearbook, and enterprise entry data sourced from industrial and commercial registration statistics68. The sample period ranges from 2010 to 2020.

Summary statistics

Descriptive statistics show that the mean per capita GDP of impoverished counties is 21,484 yuan (SD = 12,091 yuan). Rural residents’ per capita disposable income in these counties averages 7265 yuan—only about one-third of the per capita GDP. Nationally, the mean per capita GDP of China’s counties over the same period was 41,506 yuan, significantly higher than that of the sample counties, reflecting their generally poor economic status. In terms of industrial structure, the mean proportion of added value from the secondary industry is 0.359 (SD = 0.15), indicating that the secondary industry’s contribution to local economic growth remains insufficient. For fiscal balance, the mean public revenue was 409.82 million yuan, while the mean expenditure reached 2344.67 million yuan, yielding an expenditure-to-revenue ratio of 5.72 and highlighting substantial fiscal deficit pressures. Regarding enterprise growth, the mean annual number of newly registered enterprises was 2346 (SD = 2544), suggesting uneven regional growth in new enterprises. Details of summary statistics can be found in Supplementary Table 4.

Event setting

This study focuses on the impoverished counties, treating the implementation of the PPAP as a quasi-natural experiment. Among 832 impoverished counties, 236 listed in “13th Five-Year Plan”15 are designated as the treatment group, with the remaining counties serving as the control group. Impoverished counties are chosen as analytical units to ensure baseline similarity in pre-treatment conditions between treatment and control groups, thereby mitigating omitted variable bias and enabling unbiased identification.

The research window ends in 2020 for two key reasons. First, in late 2019, China released the plan for the second batch of the 13th Five-Year Plan photovoltaic poverty alleviation projects16. However, as this additional policy (might be adopted by some control groups) did not publicly specify its covered counties, it risks biasing the estimation of the 2017 policy’s effects, potentially understating its true impact. Second, since 2020, most regions in China have experienced COVID-19 disruptions, with subsequent economic and environmental indicators directly affected by other factors69,70, posing significant risks to our estimates. For these reasons, we set the research window’s endpoint at 2020.

Identification strategies

This study exploits the policy implementation as a quasi-natural experiment involving 832 impoverished counties and employs a DID design to estimate the policy effect. We designated the 236 counties listed in “13th Five-Year Plan”15 as the intervention group exposed to the policy, while the remaining 596 counties served as the comparison group to control for underlying secular changes in outcomes. The validity of this identification strategy hinges on the parallel trends assumption, which posits that in the absence of the PPAP’s targeted support, the economic and environmental trajectories of the treated counties would have evolved identically to those of the unexposed group; therefore, significant post-policy divergence in the treatment group’s outcomes from this counterfactual trend can be attributed to the causal effect of the policy71. Some concerns exist regarding these assumptions, which we address through additional analysis in Supplementary Fig. 4-7 and Supplementary Table 4.

Difference-in-differences (DID)

Model specification is defined as follows:

$${Y}_{i,t}={\alpha }_{0}+\beta \,{\text{Policy}}_{i,t}+{\lambda }_{i}+{\phi }_{t}+\gamma {Z}_{i,t}+{\varepsilon }_{i,t}$$

(1)

$${\text{Policy}}_{i,t}={\text{Treat}}_{i}\times {\text{Post}}_{t},$$

where the subscript \(i\) indicates county and \(t\) indicates the year. The dependent variable \({Y}_{i,t}\) represents either GDP or a pollution indicator in our analysis. The key independent variable is the interaction term \({\text{Treat}}_{i}\times {\text{Post}}_{t}\) where \({{\rm{Treat}}}_{i}\) is a dummy variable equal to 1 if county \(i\) is covered by the policy, and 0 otherwise. \({\text{Post}}_{t}\) is a time dummy equal to 1 for observations in or after the policy implementation year (2018), and 0 otherwise. This interaction term indicates whether county \(i\) is affected by the policy in year \(t\). What we aim to identify is \(\beta\), the coefficient of the interaction term, which captures the causal effect of the policy intervention on the dependent variable. In the baseline regression specification, we control for county-fixed effects \({\lambda }_{i}\) to capture time-invariant differences across individual units and address omitted variable bias. We also control year-fixed effects \({\phi }_{t}\) to account for time-varying shocks that are common across all counties. In addition, we include a vector of time-varying county-level characteristics \({Z}_{i,t}\) as control variables to rule out confounding factors. These control variables include the share of secondary industry in GDP growth, the share of primary industry in GDP growth, government expenditure and revenue, per capita administrative land area, and the total loan balances of financial institutions. Finally, \({\varepsilon }_{i,t}\) denotes the idiosyncratic error term.

Event study analysis

DID design requires the parallel trends assumption, a key condition that treatment and control groups should follow similar trends if there is no policy intervention. We use the event-study approach to support this assumption by analyzing their trends in the pre- policy period. We introduce \({{\rm{Implement}}}_{i,t}^{j}\) to capture the effect of the event in each period. If our assumption holds, the divergence between the trends of two groups should only emerge after policy implementation, with no significant pre-policy trend differences. We estimate:

$${Y}_{i,t}={\alpha }_{0}+\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j=\underline{j}}^{\bar{j}}{\beta }_{j}{\mathrm{Implement}}\,_{i,t}^{j}+{\lambda }_{i}+{\phi }_{t}+\gamma {Z}_{i,t}+{\varepsilon }_{i,t}$$

(2)

$${\mathrm{Implement}}_{i,t}^{j}=\left\{\begin{array}{l}\,1\,{if}\,t-j={\mathrm{Event}}\\ \,0\,{if}\,t-j\ne {\mathrm{Event}}.\hfill\end{array}\right.$$

Here, \({\mathrm{Implement}}_{i,t}^{j}\) is a dummy variable: it takes the value of 1 if the photovoltaic policy was implemented in pilot county \(i\) in year \((t-j)\), and 0 otherwise. For example, if the policy was implemented in 2017 (Event = 2017), and since \(2019-2=\mathrm{Event}\), then \({\mathrm{Implement}}_{i,2019}^{2}=1\). Therefore, \({\beta }_{0}\) captures the contemporaneous effect of policy implementation in the year of implementation; \({\beta }_{-8}\) to \({\beta }_{-1}\) measure the impacts of the policy 1 to 8 years prior to implementation, and \({\beta }_{1}\) to \({\beta }_{2}\) measure the effects 1 to 2 years after implementation. The year immediately preceding policy implementation serves as the benchmark year in the model. If \({\beta }_{-8}\) to \({\beta }_{-1}\) are statistically significant, this suggests that the parallel trends assumption is violated, and the overall results may be driven by selection bias, rendering the control group an invalid counterfactual for the treatment group. Finally, \({\beta }_{0}\) to \({\beta }_{2}\) capture the dynamic effects of the photovoltaic policy over time.

Propensity score matching (PSM)

In our research design, policy coverage may depend on various factors, and we cannot rule out potential selection bias. We adopted the Propensity Score Matching (PSM) to mitigate this concern. PSM is a widely used causal inference technique for reducing selection bias. Its main purpose is to align key covariates between treatment and control groups by matching observational data. This process approximates quasi-random experiment conditions, improving the reliability of causal effect estimates. We utilize nearest-neighbor PSM to compare treated and control counties with similar characteristics72.

In the application of the PSM model, the first step involves identifying variables that may differ between the treatment and control groups. These form a set of matching covariates, denoted as \(({x=x}_{1},{x}_{2},\cdots ,{x}_{n})\). Next, a parametric regression is performed on the binary treatment variable \({\rm{Treat}}\) using the covariate set \(x\). This is achieved via a logit regression, as illustrated in Eq. (3):

$${\rm{logit}}({\rm{Treat}})={x}^{{\prime} }\beta +\epsilon .$$

(3)

Using the regression coefficient matrix \(\beta\) derived from Eq. (3), the propensity score (\({\rm{ps}}\)) can be calculated via Eq. (4).

$${{\rm{ps}}}_{i}=\frac{\exp ({x}_{i}^{{\prime} }\beta )}{1+\exp ({x}_{i}^{{\prime} }\beta )}.$$

(4)

Here, \({x}_{i}\) represents the set of matching covariates for county \(i\). The fundamental purpose of Eq. (4) is to synthesize multidimensional matching covariates into a single, one-dimensional variable \({{\rm{ps}}}_{i}\) ranging between [0,1], which represents the probability of county \(i\) being assigned to the treatment group. Subsequently, for each county in the treatment group, we match it with two counties from the control group that have the closest \({ps}\) values to form a new control group. A new matched sample is constructed through this matching strategy. Finally, a comparison is made between the matched sample to identify the differences in outcomes. We then re-estimated the main regression using a PSM-DID model73,74. The workflow is presented in Supplementary Fig. 8. Further analysis of the matching quality is provided in Supplementary Fig. 9. The regression results for Eq. (3) are reported in Supplementary Tables 6–9.

The matching characteristics include: (1) GDP growth structure: We consider the secondary industry’s contribution to GDP growth and the primary industry’s contribution to GDP growth, as this helps reveal electricity market demand and employment needs, also related to the economy and environment. (2) Fiscal conditions: We include government revenue and expenditure, which reflect budgetary capacities. PPAP implementation requires substantial government investment, and local fiscal conditions are likely to determine participation. (3) Population density: We use per capita administrative land area to reflect population density in county-level regions, as local initial environments and economic development are directly linked to population density. (4) Financial markets: We use total loan balances of financial institutions to assess local capital market conditions. As another major funding source for PPAP, local financial institutions influence participation. (5) Environmental factors: We use annual average rainfall to reflect local climate conditions, as areas with lower rainfall are more likely to participate in PPAP.

Intensity-varying treatment effect

To account for variations in policy implementation intensity, we adopt a generalized DID model75,76. Specifically, we replace the binary policy indicator with an interaction term that captures both policy exposure and its intensity, where intensity is measured by the number of power stations, installed capacity, the number of households supported, and village-level coverage. This specification enables a more nuanced and interpretable estimation of policy effects.

$${Y}_{i,t}={\alpha }_{0}+\beta {{\rm{Intensity}}}_{i}\times {{\rm{Policy}}}_{i,t}+{\lambda }_{i}+{\phi }_{t}+\gamma {Z}_{i,t}+{\varepsilon }_{i,t}$$

(5)

$${{\rm{Policy}}}_{i,t}=\,{{\rm{Treat}}}_{i}\times \,{{\rm{Post}}}_{t},$$

where the subscript \(i\) denotes the county and \(t\) denotes the year. The dependent variable \({Y}_{i,t}\) represents either GDP or a pollution indicator. The key independent variable is the interaction term \({{\rm{Intensity}}}_{i}\times {{\rm{Policy}}}_{i,t}\), where \({\mathrm{Intensity}}_{i}\) measures policy exposure or infrastructure investment. \({{\rm{Policy}}}_{i,t}\) is a dummy variable that takes 1 if county \(i\) is covered by the policy and t is after the policy’s implementation year (2018), 0 otherwise. Our goal is to identify \(\beta\), the coefficient of this interaction term, which captures the causal effect of the policy on the dependent variable. In the baseline regression model, we control county-fixed effects \({\lambda }_{i}\) year-fixed effects \({\phi }_{t}\), and a set of time-varying county characteristics \({Z}_{i,t}\). These controls include secondary industry’s share of GDP growth, primary industry’s share of GDP growth, government expenditure and revenue, per capita administrative land area, and the total loan balances of financial institutions. Finally, \({\varepsilon }_{i,t}\) is the idiosyncratic error term.

text:
Portland, Oregon's Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund has provided over 20,000 free air conditioning units to low-income households, funded energy efficiency retrofits for 3,100 homes and trained 2,000 people in renewable energy and construction jobs, reports Monica Samayoa for Oregon Public Broadcasting.

As Samayoa explains, "The Portland Clean Energy Fund is a first-of-its-kind racial, social and climate justice fund aimed at helping the city’s most vulnerable residents adapt to climate change while also reducing carbon emissions." The fund was approved by a public measure in 2018 that levied a 1% retail sales tax — paid by the companies — on large corporations within Portland city limits. The fund has since generated roughly $1 billion for climate resilience projects. "Since 2021, the fund has distributed four rounds of community-based nonprofit grants totaling about $262 million. Grants range from about $8,000 to as high as $10.3 million — and many projects are also helping reduce greenhouse gas emissions."

Other cities are starting to replicate Portland's model, but some have local restrictions that prevent the creation of a similar retail tax. Denver passed a consumer-facing 0.25% sales tax that generated $41 million for its Climate Protection Fund. Ann Arbor increased property taxes to generate funding for climate action.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy opened a new funding opportunity offering up to $2.5 million in direct project support and about $1 million in technical assistance to support microgrid development in remote and isolated regions, including tribal communities.

The program, administered by DOE’s Community Microgrid Assistance Partnership, or C-MAP, will support projects designed to improve electric reliability in areas with high energy costs and weak grid performance. DOE said the grant opportunity focuses on microgrids that can operate independently or alongside a larger grid during outages.

“America’s remote industries play an essential role in our national prosperity,” said Dan Ton, DOE’s microgrid research and development program manager. He said the program is intended to help deliver more dependable power in remote regions while supporting “new investment, stronger local economies and expanded opportunities” for local workforces.

The grant solicitation emphasizes projects tied to industrial development and large energy users, including critical mineral operations and enterprise-scale computing centers. DOE said stronger microgrid infrastructure can help support industrial, commercial, public safety and national security facilities in remote regions.

Selected projects will receive between $200,000 and $575,000 in direct funding, along with up to 24 months of technical and administrative support from national laboratories and community partners. Eligible applicants include federally recognized tribes, Alaska Native villages and corporations, local governments, nonprofits and energy cooperatives.

Applications are due July 2, 2026. Proposed projects must serve communities with 10,000 or fewer where electricity prices are high. DOE will host an informational webinar on the funding opportunity May 26.

description:

text:
In the same week that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced that it would give Pennsylvania more than $39 million to address PFAS contamination in drinking water, the agency also said it would roll back PFAS regulations.

PFAS, also known as perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a group of thousands of chemicals used in consumer goods, including stain-resistant rugs, waterproof clothing, nonstick pans and firefighting foam. They’re called “forever chemicals” because they don’t break down, accumulating in the environment, including waterways, and the human body. PFAS are linked to developmental delays in children, some cancers, and other health issues.

PFAS were found in 76% of rivers and streams around Pennsylvania surveyed by the U.S. Geological Survey. They have contaminated drinking supplies in the Lehigh Valley, and “alarming levels” of PFAS from the Pittsburgh International Airport were found to be discharging into the Montour Run watershed.

“Addressing them is not optional. It is essential to making America healthy again,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. He was joined at a roundtable event this week with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy, Jr., who brought the Make America Healthy Again movement into Trump’s voting base.

Under Zeldin’s plan, the EPA will repeal limits on four types of PFAS, including some that have contaminated drinking water sources. The agency will also give utilities an additional two years to meet the remaining PFAS limits.

Meanwhile, the $39 million EPA grant for Pennsylvania is “for communities, drinking water systems, and private well owners to help with testing, planning, and infrastructure projects addressing PFAS and other emerging contaminants,” according to the EPA press release. The funds are from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law passed under the Biden administration.

“It feels like a real hypocrisy,” said Steve Hvozdovich, of the non-profit Clean Water Action in Pennsylvania. “[The administration is saying], ‘We’re going to give you money to deal with this threat from a toxic chemical, but at the same time we’re going to roll back protections … we’re ripping away the safeguards and protections that exist around drinking water for the very same constituents,’” he said.

Zeldin said his agency will create new, what he calls, more legally-sound PFAS regulations. Chemical makers have already sued the federal government over the PFAS drinking water standards. “This regulation from the Biden administration would not stand a court challenge,” Zeldin said.

Hvozdovich doesn’t want Pennsylvania to wait for the EPA to create new regulations. Currently, the state’s PFAS regulations allow significantly more contamination than the Biden-EPA standards.

There are bipartisan bills in the state legislature, including one to limit the use of firefighting foam containing PFAS.

The launch further strengthens TCL Zhonghuan's position in next-generation PV technology and underscores its commitment to driving higher efficiency, greater reliability, and lower lifecycle energy costs across the solar industry.

Advancing BC Technology Through Integrated Innovation

Unlike conventional BC products available in the market, TCL Zhonghuan's BC platform is built on a fully integrated technology foundation spanning wafers, cells, and modules. The company's competitive advantages include a robust portfolio of more than 1,600 foundational BC patents, dedicated BC wafer development, and decades of research and manufacturing expertise.

Combined with an optimized cell design, the technology supports conversion efficiencies exceeding 27% at the cell level while maintaining a temperature coefficient as low as -0.26%/°C.

To further enhance system reliability, TCL Zhonghuan has introduced a next-generation hotspot mitigation design that can reduce hotspot temperatures by up to 50°C compared with conventional modules. The modules also demonstrate excellent low-irradiance performance, with a weak-light response factor exceeding 95%, enabling stable energy generation under diverse operating conditions.

Setting a New Benchmark for High-Efficiency Modules

The new N-type BC modules combine TCL Zhonghuan's proprietary N-type wafer technology with advanced BC cell architecture, delivering strong performance across multiple dimensions.

With a mass-production efficiency of up to 25.2% and maximum power output reaching 680W, the modules are on par with mainstream BC products in terms of power rating. They incorporate enhanced resistance to fire risk, partial shading, and dust accumulation, while offering a 30-year linear power warranty and a 15-year product warranty.

name: Clean Energy
title: Shifting from fossil fuels will fail without funding for African industry and energy infrastructure
description:
This was the argument that African countries put to a recent meeting of 57 governments on phasing out fossil fuels.
From cutting emissions to ending fossil fuel extraction The conference called on governments to move beyond reducing greenhouse gas emissions and begin confronting the harder question of ending fossil fuel extraction.
Without meaningful financial support, many African countries may struggle to move beyond fossil fuels while maintaining jobs, government revenue and energy access.
What the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels meant for Africa The conference in Santa Marta, Colombia did not settle the future of fossil fuel governance.
It made clear that governments cannot seriously tackle emissions while continuing to treat fossil fuel extraction as a side issue.
text:
Moving to renewable energy will fail unless wealthy nations help finance cleaner energy systems, industrialisation and local mineral processing across the African continent. This was the argument that African countries put to a recent meeting of 57 governments on phasing out fossil fuels.

The Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands and held in Colombia in April 2026, was the first major international gathering focused specifically on how countries might gradually reduce their dependence on coal, oil and gas. At present, there is no global agreement on how to wind down down fossil fuel production.

Read more: African countries shouldn’t have to borrow money to fix climate damage they never caused – economist

International climate agreements focus mainly on reducing emissions rather than deciding how and when countries should stop producing coal, oil and gas. Yet these fossil fuels are responsible for almost 90% of the carbon emissions driving climate change.

I am an international trade lawyer and legal academic whose research focuses on the intersection of climate change, trade policy and sustainable development. I see Africa becoming a key site of debate over how the transition should be managed in countries that are seeking to rapidly industrialise yet highly exposed to climate disasters.

Read more: Kenya’s double climate crisis: it needs funds to adapt, and disaster aid is damaging the environment

For African countries, moving away from fossil fuels is far more complicated than simply switching energy sources. Many of them suffer from poverty, weak electricity systems, and mounting debt. Their economies still depend on oil, gas and coal for government revenue, exports, jobs and even basic energy access.

Wealthier economies industrialised using fossil fuels over many decades. Asking African states to stop producing oil and gas without substantial financial support, affordable technology and credible alternatives would therefore risk deepening inequality.

From cutting emissions to ending fossil fuel extraction

The conference called on governments to move beyond reducing greenhouse gas emissions and begin confronting the harder question of ending fossil fuel extraction. About half of the global fossil fuel producers also attended the conference (including those from Nigeria and Angola).

This was a significant step towards working out how countries can stop using fossil fuels. Many countries have pledged to limit global warming but continue to approve new oil and gas projects and subsidise fossil fuel production.

For example, the Nigerian government wants to almost double oil output over the next five years and increase gas production. South Africa also wants to increase gas production. Because it set up a state-owned petroleum company, it will likely expand petrol production too.

Read more: Nigeria and South Africa plan to boost fossil fuel production, risking their climate change pledges

A “supply side” agreement could work. The Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty that 18 states and thousands of civil society organisations have so far endorsed wants to commit states to lowering the production of coal, oil and gas.

In practical terms, it would encourage countries to plan for a managed transition away from fossil fuels rather than expanding production indefinitely.

A just transition needs investment, not lectures

For African countries to transition to clean energy, they’d need to do without the revenues they get from selling fossil fuels. They’d also have to restructure their economies beyond the current global fossil fuel dependency.

This dependence is substantial. Fossil fuels account for over 90% of export earnings in countries such as Nigeria and Angola.

Oil and gas revenues provide between 50% and 70% of government income in several states across the continent. Any abrupt transition without alternative sources of growth and finance will be economically disruptive.

Read more: Climate finance has failed Africa twice over – how to fix it

Countries cannot be left to fend for themselves when global trade and energy systems are deeply interconnected. Africa already faces a climate financing shortfall of about US$2.5 trillion by 2030. It would not be just to ask African countries to pay for the transition themselves. This would amount to adjustment without solidarity.

Without meaningful financial support, many African countries may struggle to move beyond fossil fuels while maintaining jobs, government revenue and energy access.

Africa must build green energy industries

What Africa needs is not charity, but investment in credible projects. These include renewable power, electricity grids, battery assembly, clean cooking, and public transport, among others. These green energy industries would create jobs and long-term economic value on the African continent.

Africa already has many of the ingredients needed for this shift. The continent has abundant solar and wind resources, growing markets and a young workforce. Some African countries also have the minerals needed for clean energy technologies. But success will depend on using these advantages to build industries at home.

Read more: Why Africa needs a green bank to fund climate action and build its own renewable technology

Countries will also need stronger infrastructure, stable regulations, and investment in technical skills. If properly managed, the energy transition could help Africa industrialise in cleaner ways that do not exacerbate the climate crisis. But without deliberate planning and financing, the continent risks remaining a consumer of imported technologies rather than becoming a producer in the global green economy.

What the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels meant for Africa

The conference in Santa Marta, Colombia did not settle the future of fossil fuel governance. Its contribution is more modest – but still important. It made clear that governments cannot seriously tackle emissions while continuing to treat fossil fuel extraction as a side issue.

Read more: South Africa needs R250 billion just to meet basic climate adaptation needs over the next decade

For Africa, the task is not to resist transition. It is to insist that transition be financed, sequenced and governed fairly.

text:
Imagine a city where every breath is cleaner and safer. For millions living in the world’s busiest urban centers, that vision may seem out of reach. However, advances in ambient air quality monitoring are bringing it closer to reality.

As urban populations continue to grow, the need to monitor and improve air quality has never been more urgent. This article explores the science behind ambient air quality monitoring and the transformative impact these technologies can have on public health and urban environments.

Image credit: Oatawa/Shutterstock.com

The Urban Challenge

Urban regions are lively centers for culture, innovation, and community. However, they face unique environmental concerns.

Traffic congestion, industrial activity, and large population densities all contribute to air pollution levels that can exceed health-based air quality standards. Urban inhabitants are often exposed to particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, and other hazardous pollutants.

Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is one of several extremely reactive gases known as nitrogen oxides or NOx. The primary source of NO2 in the atmosphere is fuel combustion: emissions from automobiles, trucks, and buses, as well as power plants and off-road equipment, produce NO2.

The US Environmental Protection Agency states that:

Breathing air with a high concentration of NO2 can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Such exposures over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions and visits to emergency rooms. Longer exposures to elevated concentrations of NO2 may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections.

Understanding and controlling these contaminants necessitates a thorough monitoring strategy that can decipher the intricate tapestry of urban air quality.

The Science of Air Quality Monitoring

The science of air quality monitoring is fundamental to improving urban air quality. This method involves collecting and analyzing air samples to determine the amounts of various pollutants. Both traditional and cutting-edge technologies are used to detect anything from tiny amounts of nitrogen dioxide to large levels of particulate matter.

Depending on the type of gas being monitored and the intended data output, numerous air quality monitoring and analysis systems have been proved to efficiently analyze ambient air and detect its components, including:

Optically Enhanced Fourier Transform Infrared (OE-FTIR)

Non-Dispersive Infrared (NDIR) Technology

Pulsed Fluorescence Technology

Gas Chromatography (GC)

Gas Filter Correlation (GFC)

Chemiluminescence

Gas Scrubbing

UV Photometry

Innovations in data distribution methods and sensor design have also played important roles in providing more precise, real-time insights into the air we breathe. These developments provide a clearer understanding of pollution sources and trends, allowing for more effective treatments.

Global Efforts and Innovations

Cities around the world are turning to science and technology to revitalize their efforts to improve air quality. From London's Ultra Low Emission Zone to Seoul's network of air quality sensors, cities use a combination of policy and technology to battle air pollution.

These efforts frequently use real-time data to inform politicians and the public alike, resulting in improvements ranging from traffic management tactics to industrial pollution limits. Such programs highlight technology's ability to monitor and drive action for better air.

The Impact on Communities

The benefits of cleaner air go far beyond the environment, affecting every area of urban life. Improved air quality has a huge public health impact, lowering the incidence of respiratory disorders, cardiovascular ailments, and other pollution-related health problems.

The importance of effective air quality monitoring goes beyond creating a healthier and more sustainable urban environment. It is also crucial for understanding the specific applications of various monitoring tools and how they can provide accurate data so cities and communities can track air quality trends and make informed decisions.

As communities become increasingly involved in monitoring and improving air quality, they also become change agents, contributing to a global push for cleaner, healthier cities.

Conclusion

The quest for cleaner urban air is a multidisciplinary challenge that requires the collaborative efforts of scientists, policymakers, and residents. Air quality monitoring not only provides insights into environmental health, but also methods for improving it.

As solutions continue to be discovered and deployed, the dream of easy breathing in cities becomes increasingly realistic. By being aware and engaged, we can all help to clear the air for future generations.

Unlike conventional BC products available in the market, TCL Zhonghuan's BC platform is built on a fully integrated technology foundation spanning wafers, cells, and modules.
